Event-driven detectors offer an efficient alternative by representing the measurement as a sparse stream of individual incidences, substantially reducing requirements related to data handling and enabling on-the-fly processing. Here, we develop a high-throughput, real-time, 4D-STEM workflow based on the Timepix4 detector and demonstrate its operation at microsecond dwell times and standard beam currents. A common clock shared by the scan unit and detector allows the probe position of each electron event to be determined directly from its time-of-arrival, eliminating the need for inter-stream synchronization and enabling fully concurrent and independent multi-stream processing. The resulting pipeline continuously processes the detector data during acquisition, with the reconstructed images directly available. We demonstrate live virtual annular detector imaging, Real-Time Integration Center of Mass and direct electron ptychography within the guided progressive reconstructive imaging framework. The workflow sustains the high event rates of Timepix4 while maintaining zero latency for live interactive operation, thus extending event-driven 4D-STEM towards beam currents and acquisition conditions beyond those previously demonstrated with Timepix3-based systems. These results demonstrate that the combination of high-bandwidth event-driven detection, hardware-level synchronization and parallel processing can transform 4D-STEM from an offline technique into an interactive imaging modality, in which dose-efficient phase contrast and diffraction-based signals can serve directly as immediate feedback during STEM experiments.

papers.title: AdaptaFace: Adversarial Assistance for Inclusive Facial Gesture Interaction
papers.summary: Facial gestures can enable access for people with motor impairments (PwM), yet recognizers may not reliably interpret individual facial movement patterns. Existing approaches either constrain agency by requiring predefined templates or impose repeated calibration, data collection, and computation through user-specific retraining. We present AdaptaFace, an input-level compatibility layer using bounded, proxy-dependent adversarial perturbations to translate user-compatible gestures into inputs for an unchanged facial action unit (AU)-based recognizer. Designed around six personalization principles informed by interviews with 12 PwM, AdaptaFace supports both recognition enhancement and gesture vocabulary extension. In a within-subject study with 16 participants, AdaptaFace increased task completion from 59.7% to 90.5% and reduced workload from 5.61 to 4.21. Offline validation showed strong steering with aligned perturbation generation and evaluation but weaker cross-recognizer transfer, defining the approach's boundary. These findings frame adversarial assistance as input-side accessibility mediation for personalized facial-gesture interaction.

papers.title: Diagnose Before You Refine: Multi-Dimensional Judge Feedback for Query-Efficient Jailbreak Attacks
papers.summary: Automated jailbreak attacks rely on evaluation feedback to optimize adversarial prompts, but existing methods often lack fine-grained diagnostic information. We propose Jev-Guided Strategy Bandit (JSB), a query-based jailbreak framework that leverages multi-dimensional probabilistic feedback to guide prompt optimization. JSB combines continuous jailbreak scoring with targeted refinement, strategy switching, and best-state reseeding to balance exploration and refinement. We evaluate JSB on two harmful request datasets across five open-source and three closed-source LLMs. Under a budget of only 10 target-model queries, JSB achieves an average HarmBench attack success rate of 89.8\% across ten open-source settings, consistently outperforming existing automated jailbreak attacks. Further analyses demonstrate its effectiveness under varying query budgets and attacker models. Defense experiments also reveal limitations in existing filtering mechanisms and highlight the potential of Jev-based output filtering.

papers.title: Preservation of photon statistics upon selective molecular modulation in hollow-core fibers
papers.summary: Preserving the underlying statistical properties of light during frequency transduction is essential for interfacing spectrally disparate quantum systems. To do this successfully, the process needs to be highly efficient, broadband and noiseless. Despite significant progress in this field, satisfying all these conditions remains challenging. Recently, molecular modulation-based transduction in hollow-core fibers has emerged as a promising approach, where biphoton correlations were proven to be preserved during frequency up-conversion. However, beyond this previous demonstration of correlation-maintaining conversion, whether molecular modulation can preserve more general statistical properties of light remains experimentally unexplored. Here, we demonstrate the conservation of photon-number statistics during selective frequency transduction by Raman molecular modulation in a hydrogen-filled hollow-core fiber. As a proof of concept, weak 585-nm signals are selectively converted to 773 nm in the near-infrared and to 471 nm in the blue spectral region with near-unity efficiencies. Phase matching between the generated coherence waves and the transitions of interest is achieved through the effective dispersion of the system, enabling independent selection of the frequency up- and down-conversion processes. The preservation of the photon-number statistics of the shifted signals, along with the large frequency shifts, broad tunability and compatibility with quantum-optical fields, provides a versatile fiber-based platform for quantum frequency transduction. In particular, the demonstrated interfacing between visible and near-infrared wavelengths using low pump energies and low gas pressures offers a route towards connecting spectrally distinct quantum systems, including quantum emitters, sensors and atomic quantum memories, within hybrid quantum networks.

papers.title: Testing graph isomorphism using simple quantum circuits
papers.summary: The graph isomorphism problem asks whether two graphs are equivalent up to a permutation of their vertices. Its precise computational complexity remains unresolved, and it is still unknown whether a polynomial-time algorithm exists. We investigate whether simple graph-dependent Instantaneous Quantum Polynomial-time (IQP) and Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm (QAOA) circuits can distinguish non-isomorphic graphs. We first show that suitable IQP and QAOA constructions allow the underlying graph to be reconstructed using a polynomial number of samples. Building on previous work using the QAOA energy, we show that Hamming weight distributions can distinguish graph pairs at circuit depths for which the numerically computed energy gap is zero. We then apply graph invariants to the matrix of ZZ correlators on the output distribution. For the specific case of the graph spectrum, at QAOA depth $p=2$, this invariant numerically distinguishes all $10{,}486$ cospectral regular graph pairs tested on up to 18 vertices. For IQP circuits, we introduce a finer invariant based on probability multiplicities within Hamming weight sectors, which distinguishes every non-isomorphic graph pair tested numerically. Finally, we derive exact graph-theoretic characterisations of the IQP output distribution at $θ=π/2$ and $θ=π/4$. These results show that simple graph-dependent quantum circuits encode substantial structural information, while leaving open whether this information can be extracted efficiently for general graph isomorphism.

papers.title: Observation of correlations beyond the single-particle picture in fermionic counting statistics
papers.summary: The analysis of charge fluctuations in a mesoscopic device can shed light on the fundamental question of whether or not a single-particle picture of electron transport is appropriate, even in the presence of Coulomb interaction. It has been shown on general grounds that mapping the interacting system onto a fermionic single-particle description is subject to strict constraints on the charge-transfer statistics. These constraints can be formulated in terms of a sign rule for the factorial cumulants of the full counting statistics. We report here on the experimental observation of a sign-rule violation in a most elementary model system, i.e. a single-level quantum dot, and provide theoretical modeling that can quantitatively reproduce the experimental data. This reveals the presence of correlations introduced by electron-electron interaction.

papers.title: Reciprocity coordinates a three-way trade-off in recurrent neural circuits
papers.summary: Biological neural circuits contain both unidirectional and reciprocal connections, but how reciprocity affects circuit computation remains unclear. We varied reciprocity \r{ho} across 21 levels in recurrent-network simulations while holding network size, connection density, and directed-edge count fixed. Low-reciprocity networks produced more diverse stimulus-driven activity and performed better on four continuous-input tasks, whereas higher reciprocity generally improved performance on three delayed-memory tasks. Increasing reciprocity reduced online memory capacity and accelerated recovery from perturbations. A post-cue noise experiment showed that higher reciprocity suppressed internal noise propagation but made cue-evoked states less distinguishable, and component matching separated the contributions of cue separation and within-cue dispersion to readout robustness. Within this ensemble, reciprocity thus mediates a three-way trade-off among representational capacity, local stability, and task-state separability: higher reciprocity lowers capacity, strengthens stability, and compresses separability. Whether it improves behaviour depends on whether the stability gain outweighs the lost separation between task states. Connectome and microcircuit datasets from five species showed intermediate reciprocity, while reciprocity varied substantially across adult Drosophila brain regions, providing compatible structural context and motivating circuit-specific functional tests.

papers.title: Quiet Triggers, Loud Footprints: A Tri-Space Measurement Study of Backdoor Stealthiness
papers.summary: Backdoor attacks on deep neural networks are commonly evaluated by attack success rate and benign accuracy, yet their stealthiness remains inconsistently defined and measured. Existing work often studies only one observable aspect of stealthiness, such as trigger imperceptibility, feature-space separability, parameter-space concentration, or evasion of particular defenses. This creates a fragmented picture: an attack may appear stealthy under one metric while leaving conspicuous footprints elsewhere. This paper presents a tri-space measurement study of backdoor stealthiness in image classification. We distinguish latent stealthiness---the ideal but unobservable difficulty of distinguishing a backdoored system from a benign one---from measurable footprints in three spaces: input, feature, and parameter space. Under this framework, we evaluate representative backdoor attacks across four datasets and three model architectures using a broad suite of footprint metrics. Our results show that stealthiness is not monolithic: attacks that are quiet in one space are often loud in another, and existing attacks rarely achieve consistently small footprints across all three spaces. We further analyze agreement and disagreement among stealthiness metrics and study how footprint measurements interact with attack success rate. Based on observed blind spots in existing measurements, we introduce two diagnostic metrics: Class-Specific Davies--Bouldin Index (CDBI), which captures class-conditional feature overlap, and TAC--UCLC Product (TUP), which identifies channels that are both trigger-responsive and downstream influential. These metrics are intended to augment, not replace, the broader measurement suite. Finally, we provide practical guidance for future stealthiness evaluations.

papers.title: Joint-measurement advantage and finite-time transitions in accelerated detector registers
papers.summary: The Unruh response thermalizes accelerated detectors, but the entanglement remaining in a register does not by itself specify what distributed measurements can recover. We study this distinction for a four-qubit cluster state whose two assisting nodes independently undergo generalized amplitude damping, while the target nodes remain isolated and the environments are inaccessible. We derive the exact joint-assisted concurrence and the exact one-way value for arbitrary local measurements. The joint optimum equals the bipartition negativity, and computational-basis measurements attain the one-way optimum. A polar-decomposition argument, together with compactness, establishes a necessary and sufficient condition for separable measurements to attain the joint optimum and proves a strict gap whenever this condition fails. For assisting detectors at equal Unruh temperature with relaxation-rate ratio $r>1$, joint advantage exists precisely when the thermal excitation factor satisfies $q<1/r$. At finite positive temperature it ends at a unique finite time, while the remaining entanglement is nonzero. For $r=2$, both the transition time and remaining resource have closed expressions. These results identify when joint assistance is necessary within the independent weak-coupling thermalization model.

papers.title: Quantum noise and torque correlations in a torsion-bar Sagnac speed meter
papers.summary: Quantum fluctuations entering through weakly transmitting mirrors can limit a torsion-bar Sagnac speed meter for low-frequency gravitational-wave detection, even when its optical layout suppresses radiation-pressure back action. We show that, in the Cryogenic sub-Hz cROss torsion bar detector with quantum NOn-demolition Speed meter (CHRONOS), vacuum fields entering from behind the end and middle test masses can dominate the low-frequency quantum noise despite cancellation of the torques on opposite ends of each bar. For a reference configuration with mirror power transmissions of only $10^{-7}$, these fields contribute $89.7\%$ of the total quantum-noise power spectral density at 0.1 Hz. Omitting them would underestimate the amplitude spectral density by a factor of 3.11. Our input-output model connects the correlations produced by successive optical interactions to the forces on each bar and the measured signal. This connection shows why strong torque cancellation does not, by itself, ensure a corresponding improvement in detector sensitivity. Replacing mirror transmission with absorption at fixed reflectivity leaves the excess quantum noise essentially unchanged for the two operating points studied. The predicted signal response and quantum noise agree with independent FINESSE 3 calculations as recycling detuning and homodyne angle are varied. These results establish rear vacuum fields as a limiting noise source in this torsion-bar speed meter and provide quantitative requirements for its mirror and readout design.

papers.title: Improved Quantum Algorithms for Rényi Entropies Estimation
papers.summary: Entropy estimation of discrete probability distributions is a fundamental problem in statistical inference and quantum property estimation. In this paper, we study the problem of estimating Rényi entropy $H_α(\mathbf{p})$ for any distribution $\mathbf{p} = (p_i)_{i=1}^n$ given its purified quantum query-access. For non-integer $α> 1$, our algorithm estimates $H_α(\mathbf{p})$ to within additive error $ε$ using only $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\big(n^{\max\{1/2,1-1/α\}}/ε\big)$ queries, which improves the best known upper bound for dependence on both $n$ and $1/ε$. For $0<α<1$, our algorithm has query complexity $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\big(n^{1/(2α)}/ε^{\max\{1,1/(2α)\}}\big)$, which improves the dependence on $1/ε$ of the current best upper bound without incresing its $n$ dependence. Our approach adapts the multi-level estimation framework to relative approximation of the power sums and leverage binary search to remove the requirement of prior knowledge of them. We also strengthen the precision-dependent lower bound to $Ω\big(1/ε^{\max\{1,1/(2α)\}}\big)$ for $0<α<1$, which identifies the optimal precision dependence of our algorithm.
papers.comment: Improved Rényi entropy estimator for integer $α$ to be added

papers.title: Photon Demultiplexing Using Spatial Routing
papers.summary: Spatial sectioning of the far-field noncollinear field from spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) is a promising approach for multiparty quantum communication. Although demonstrations with six pairs of users have been reported, the fundamental limits remain unknown. These include the maximum number of channels, the required degree of channel optimization, and the dependence on input parameters. In this paper, we provide a practical framework that answers these questions by connecting input parameters and invoking a design theorem. For a representative configuration, we realize 12 user-pair channels with routing consistency exceeding $0.9999$ at a $12\%$ reduction in photon flux. We further show that sectioning improves the accidental-coincidence budget linearly with the number of channels $N$, allowing the aggregate key rate to scale with the user count. These results provide a design strategy for spatial-division multiplexing of entangled photons analogous to the channel-spacing standards used in wavelength-division networks.

papers.title: Improved Forecasting for Multivariate Time Series using GNAR models with General Inverse Distance Weights
papers.summary: Many multivariate time series arise on networks where relationships between variables depend on physical or more general distances. Standard vector autoregressive models struggle in such settings due to their quadratic parameter growth, while generalised network autoregressive (GNAR) models offer a parsimonious alternative by explicitly incorporating network structures. Existing GNAR formulations assume fixed weights, typically uniform or reciprocal distances, which may not reflect the true influence of distance in real systems. We introduce a novel model with general inverse distance weights (GNARID) that extends GNAR by introducing a tunable exponent parameter that controls the strength of distance penalisation. We establish theoretical results on the consistency and asymptotic normality of new GNARID estimators, including an extension to the setting where the number of nodes grows. We analyse the effect of misspecifying the exponent on forecasting error, which helps assess how much GNAR models could be improved by our tunable weights. Simulation studies confirm the theoretical properties and show measurable benefits from correct weight specification. Using the Brumadinho ground displacement dataset, we show that proper tuning of the weight exponent improves predictive performance, highlighting the practical value of flexible distance-based weighting in network time series models.

papers.title: A New Perspective on Cumulative Residual Rényi Entropy
papers.summary: This paper introduces a new cumulative residual Rényi entropy (CRRE), which addresses limitations of the existing cumulative residual Rényi entropy. The conventional measure suffers from two primary drawbacks: its failure to converge to the cumulative residual entropy (CRE) as the order parameter approaches unity, and its lack of guaranteed positivity. Our proposed CRRE resolves these issues, offering a theoretically consistent and always nonnegative measure of uncertainty in residual lifetimes. We explore its mathematical properties, including its relationship with existing information measures. Furthermore, the concept is extended to its dynamic version, and its time-dependent characteristics are investigated. A non-parametric estimator of the proposed CRRE is developed, its almost sure convergence is established, and is validated through Monte Carlo simulation. The effectiveness of CRRE as a tool for quantifying uncertainty is confirmed through its application in chaotic theory and financial data.

papers.title: Bilinear Compressive Security with Finitely Many Samples
papers.summary: Bilinear Compressive Security (BCS) is a lightweight encryption scheme that combines compressed sensing with a fresh random convolution filter to improve resistance against key-recovery attacks under key reuse. Previous work derived information-theoretic guarantees for BCS by relating key identifiability to phase retrieval under the assumption that an adversary has access to the full ciphertext distribution induced by the random filter. In practice, however, an adversary only observes finitely many encryptions, leaving the security of BCS in the finite-sample regime largely unexplored. In this paper, we study key recovery from only finitely many observations. We first develop a covariance-based attack that estimates the linear measurements from repeated encryptions of the same plaintext and subsequently recovers the secret measurement matrix. We analyze the estimation procedure and derive finite-sample guarantees together with corresponding sample-complexity bounds. We further investigate the complete attack experimentally and compare its observed recovery behavior with the previously established information-theoretic identifiability results. Our experiments show two qualitatively different recovery regimes on the structure of the measurement matrix. For dense matrices, including Gaussian matrices, the number of measurements required for successful recovery appears to grow linearly with the signal dimension. This differs from the worst-case behavior suggested by information theory. In contrast, for matrices with sparse rows, we observe a quadratic growth consistent with the theoretical bound. These results suggest that the sparsity structure of the measurement matrix plays an important role in the security of BCS and should be taken into account when selecting parameters and designing practical instances of the scheme.

papers.title: Maximum likelihood, neural networks and posterior mean for inferring fractional Brownian motion parameters
papers.summary: Fractional Brownian motion (fBM) is a model of anomalous diffusion parameterised by a Hurst exponent $H \in (0,1)$ and a generalised diffusion coefficient $D_H > 0$. We jointly estimate $H$ and $D_H$ using maximum likelihood (MLE) from density measurements with Poisson counting noise and single-particle trajectory with Gaussian localisation error. We show that one density measurement in time cannot infer both $H$ and $D_H$ and that several time points are needed, which matters most for inference precision. For trajectories, we show that a neural network trained with a squared error loss approximates the posterior mean of $H$, which can be computed exactly at negligible cost. Paired with the profile-likelihood estimate of $D_H$, the posterior mean has the lowest root mean squared error in both $H$ and $D_H$, except near $H=0$ and $H=1$ where MLE estimates $H$ better. In vesicle trajectories from two cell types, $H$ and $D_H$ form a continuum rather than distinct modes of motion. The posterior probability that each window within a track is subdiffusive or superdiffusive shows that $26\%$ of MRC5 fibroblast and $21\%$ of HeLa vesicle trajectories contain both subdiffusive and superdiffusive windows, against $2\%$ and $7\%$ expected from estimation uncertainty alone. Intracellular cargoes therefore switch between subdiffusion and superdiffusion over time rather than forming populations with fixed $H$.

papers.title: Interactive and Robust PCA Graphics with FSDA in MATLAB
papers.summary: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a standard method for dimension reduction and the exploratory analysis of multivariate data, but a complete applied workflow often requires more than numerical eigenvectors and static plots. This article documents a set of routines in the FSDA toolbox for MATLAB that implements an integrated workflow for interactive and robust PCA graphics. The software contribution consists of coordinating classical SVD-based PCA, dynamic biplot scaling controlled by row and column parameters, score-distance and orthogonal-distance diagnostics, hard-trimming robust PCA through the Minimum Covariance Determinant and the Forward Search, linked brushing, geographical displays, and three-dimensional projection diagnostics. The implementation returns reproducible numerical output while also exposing graphical controls for changing biplot geometry, confidence regions, displayed labels, robust trimming levels, and linked selections. The methodology is illustrated on quality-of-life indicators for Italian provinces, where the software reveals variable groups, atypical provinces, robust and non-robust PCA structures, and geographical patterns. The emphasis is on statistical software: no new PCA estimator is proposed, but established PCA and robust-PCA methodology is combined in a documented, extensible, and script-reproducible MATLAB environment.

papers.title: Principal Component Analysis for Zero-Inflated Probability Measures via Lorenz Curves
papers.summary: This paper develops a principal component analysis framework for probability measures associated with non-negative real-valued random variables with structural zeros. Specifically, leveraging the associated Lorenz Curve (LC) and a suitable perspective transformation of the plane, a bijective embedding is defined to treat such measures as functional data in a Hilbert space. Once the random LC is embedded in this space, standard Functional Principal Component Analysis (FPCA) becomes directly applicable, and the diffeomorphic nature of the embedding allows the main convergence results and their interpretations to be transferred back to the original space of LC. The a.s. and $L^2(\mathbb{P})$ consistency of the estimated eigenfunctions, eigenvalues, and modes of variation is subsequently investigated, both in the embedded space and, by virtue of the embedding's diffeomorphism property, in the original LC space. Crucially, this consistency analysis accounts for the double stochasticity of the estimation problem: one level of randomness is tied to the underlying LC process itself, while the other stems from the empirical estimation of the LC from sample data. As a consequence, consistency of the Karhunen--Loève reconstructions is also established, guaranteeing faithful approximation of individual curves in both spaces. Finally, the proposed FPCA methodology is illustrated on a real-world dataset of global export flows and compared with a naive FPCA approach.

papers.title: Lost in the Fallback: How Reliably Do Typed Decision Models Use Fallback Options?
papers.summary: Typed decision models (TDMs) are increasingly used in applications such as request routing and model selection, making reliable decisions critical to system performance. Fallback options accommodate categories outside regular choices, enabling deferral to human experts or more capable models. While recent works have examined adversarial vulnerabilities in TDMs, their ability to follow fallback rules in non-adversarial settings remains underexplored. We introduce the Paired Fallback Robustness (PFR) Test to evaluate two aspects of fallback reliability: whether models correctly switch between regular and fallback options, and whether they make consistent decisions under logically equivalent definitions of the same rule. We evaluate open-source decision models on three benchmarks, with controlled comparisons across architectures and parameter counts. We find that correct recognition does not reliably transfer to correct fallback options, and errors persist even when the correct category is explicitly supplied.Moreover, logically equivalent formulations of the same fallback rule can also produce substantial disagreement in model decisions. These findings reveal a crucial reliability gap in current TDMs: fallback mechanisms designed to improve reliability can instead introduce errors. It highlights faithful execution of fallback rules and consistency under equivalent definitions as essential requirements for reliable typed decision-making.

papers.title: Global and Local Entropy Tests for STL Files Under IEEE-754 Validity Constraints
papers.summary: Shannon entropy is a standard measure of ciphertext randomness, evaluated either globally over the byte histogram of the entire ciphertext or locally as the average over non-overlapping blocks of ?xed size. While the global statistic captures only the overall byte distribution, the local statistic is also sensitive to non-randomness that is con?ned to parts of the ciphertext. Both measures are commonly assessed against reference values derived under the assumption of independent uniform bytes. However, STL encodes most numerical data as single-precision IEEE-754 ?oats, and format validity requires them to be ?nite, causing nonuniform byte probabilities and dependence between the two bytes of each exponent pair. We derive the exact mean and variance of entropy under the valid-STL (VSTL) distribution, which assigns equal probability to every admissible sequence of triangle records, and provide second-order expansions that keep the global reference values practical to compute at large ?le sizes. Using these expansions, we establish a two-sided hypothesis test for the global entropy statistic, whose limiting value is lowered from 8 to 7.99991479609 bits. The format constraints also change the local entropy reference: applying the capacity energy criterion to triangle records selects a block size of 1950 bytes instead of 1936 bytes, with an exact reference mean of 7.903106732975 rather than 7.902469316647 bits. Although small, these shifts are su?cient to place the VSTL reference means outside the conventional 95% acceptance intervals at practical ?le sizes, making unadjusted entropy tests prone to falsely rejecting ideal VSTL ciphertexts. Monte-Carlo simulations con?rm all reference values within sampling error. We therefore recommend using the format-speci?c reference values derived here to evaluate STL ciphers.

papers.title: DeltaStreamer: Towards Human-Like Agentic Streaming Video Understanding
papers.summary: We propose DeltaStreamer, a novel agentic framework for streaming video understanding inspired by how humans observe, remember, and investigate. Streaming video understanding requires a system to retain evidence before knowing which details future queries will need. Existing approaches often obscure event transitions and omit relevant details when compressing video history, and cannot recover missing visual evidence. DeltaStreamer addresses these limitations by combining change-aware memory with query-driven planning and targeted evidence gathering with replay. Before a query arrives, it continuously observes the stream and explicitly records visual changes in structured memory, preserving how events unfold rather than only what is present. When a query arrives, a query-driven planner identifies the required evidence and guides memory retrieval and targeted replay. By revisiting historical frames, the agent can recover visual details omitted during observation and ground its answer in evidence beyond the retained descriptions. This connects continuous observation with active investigation tailored to each question. Experiments on OVO-Bench and StreamingBench demonstrate improvements over representative streaming video understanding methods, with overall scores of 66.07% and 59.53%, respectively. Project page: https://bbbbchan.github.io/DeltaStreamer/

papers.title: DarKnight: Retrieval-Guided Agentic Framework for Breaking Dark Web CAPTCHA Gates
papers.summary: Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) investigators who monitor dark web marketplaces for leaked credentials and breach listings must pass the diverse CAPTCHAs that operators deploy to block automated collection. Existing solvers either need unscalable per-site fine-tuning or rely on commercial Vision-Language Model (VLM) APIs, which surrender operational sovereignty: provider policies, Tor-exit blocking, government regulation, or model updates outside the investigator's control can halt or alter the solver overnight, and per-call costs recur with every session and retry. We present DarKnight, a self-improving agentic framework designed to run on a single workstation GPU inside an investigator's Tor crawler and solve CAPTCHAs with small, locally hosted open-weight VLMs that no provider decision can withdraw, without per-market training or third-party services. For each CAPTCHA, DarKnight retrieves successful and failed past attempts on similar images (dual-signal RAG), composes an image-specific preprocessing pipeline, and learns from the site's pass/fail verdict. In a case study on four real-world dark web marketplaces, agentic tool selection outperformed parameter scaling. A deployable open-weight VLM with DarKnight reached 83.2\% on the most heavily defended market, 37.2 percentage points above its base model, outperforming even the frontier Claude Opus~5 (44%). DarKnight recovered 48.2% of baseline failures at a 7.6% degeneration cost, indicating that selective tool use can avoid much of the degradation caused by uniform preprocessing.

papers.title: Adaptive and Proximal Federated Optimization for Transferable Network Intrusion Detection
papers.summary: Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS) based on deep learning often fail to detect attack classes that are absent from training data, limiting their robustness against zero-day threats. This property called transferability across attack classes, remains underexplored especially in federated learning (FL) settings where data heterogeneity and client drift pose additional challenges. Prior work (TabFIDS) showed that FedAvg combined with bootstrapping and temporal averaging improves transferability for cross-device NIDS. In this paper, we explore whether other federated optimizers can do better. We compare two optimizers inspired by FedAdam and FedProx against the FedAvg baseline on the CIC-IDS 2017 dataset using an 11-client federated setup, sweep 10 hyperparameter configurations, and contrast two data-balancing strategies: bootstrapping and SMOTE. Using the count of client pairs whose transferred-model accuracy exceeds 70% as our primary metric (following TabFIDS), the proximal optimizer with a strong regularization term yields 48 transferable pairs versus 42 for FedAvg, while the adaptive optimizer with an aggressive server learning rate yields 46 pairs. SMOTE improves per-pair accuracy over bootstrapping but reduces breadth, revealing a depth-vs-breadth trade-off: high accuracy on a few client pairs versus moderate accuracy across most. These results indicate that the choice of federated optimizer, the rule by which client updates are regularized and aggregated into the global model, is very important for federated NIDS.

papers.title: Analyzing and Mitigating Poisoning Attacks on Flow-Based Intrusion Detection
papers.summary: Although Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs) are increasingly deployed in operational networks, their dependence on large-scale training data introduces a critical vulnerability to stealthy poisoning attacks. We demonstrate that latent backdoors can be successfully implanted in flow-based IDS models by poisoning as little as 0.001% of the training data, maintaining near-nominal performance on clean inputs while ensuring high attack success rates. To address this threat, we propose a diagnostic-first methodology that localizes trigger-relevant features through constrained perturbation analysis and detects poisoning-induced behavioral drift by comparison with a distilled baseline model. The proposed methodology further enables targeted mitigation via automated data sanitization or neuron pruning. Our findings expose the operational risks of near-undetectable backdoors and provide a scalable approach to analyzing, quantifying, and mitigating backdoor exposure in AI-based IDS.
papers.comment: 6 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Cyber Security and Resilience

papers.title: Generalized Odds for Ordinal Outcomes: A Causal Inference Framework Adjusting for Covariates
papers.summary: Background: Generalized Odds (Gen Odds) provide summaries for ordinal outcomes without requiring the proportional odds assumption. However, conventional Gen Odds compares independently drawn treatment and control outcomes and targets a population-level contrast rather than an individual-level contrast. We developed an individual-level causal formulation of Gen Odds and examined its identification. Methods: We defined the Causal Gen Odds using the joint distribution of potential outcomes and identified it under conditional independence of the potential outcomes given baseline covariates. We developed a model-based estimator using nonproportional cumulative logistic regression and introduced an odds-ratio sensitivity parameter to assess departures from conditional independence. We evaluated the estimators through simulations and illustrated them using data from the ACCORD Study. Results: In simulations, the conditional-independence estimator was approximately unbiased with 95.5% confidence interval coverage under conditional independence, but bias and undercoverage increased with residual dependence. When the sensitivity-analysis estimator incorporated the data-generating dependence parameter, bias remained below 0.01 and coverage ranged from 93.7% to 96.1% across examined settings. In the ACCORD Study, the Causal Gen Odds for right-foot pre-tibial edema was 0.909 (95% CI: 0.880 to 0.940) under conditional independence and remained stable across the examined sensitivity range. Conclusions: The Causal Gen Odds provides an individual-level estimand that complements the conventional population-level Gen Odds. This framework enables estimation of this contrast while explicitly assessing its robustness to assumptions about dependence between potential outcomes.

papers.title: ProtModernBERT: Compute-Efficient Protein Language Modeling
papers.summary: Large protein language models provide a powerful framework for learning sequence-function relationships and guiding experimental design. However, architectural improvements are underexplored, especially in low-compute regimes of relevance for resource-constrained research laboratories. We show that the training cost for encoder-only transformer architectures can be reduced by leveraging modern architectural refinements, offering an encouraging performance / compute-efficiency trade-off. We introduce ProtModernBERT, a modernized BERT-style model pre-trained on amino acid sequences, and compare it with ProtBert, Amplify, and ESM2 across a set of supervised structural tasks -encompassing secondary structure prediction, disorder prediction, and subcellular localization- and ProteinGym's zero-shot functional benchmark. We find that ProtModernBERT matches or closely tracks the performance of Amplify-120M and ProtBert with up to 80-90\% reduction in pre-training FLOPs, and narrows the gap to ESM2 when controlling for pre-training. Our analysis using a cluster-based validation protocol for hyperparameter selection and randomly initialized models disentangles the contributions of architecture and data, showing that modern components provide stronger inductive biases that are more consequential than parameter count in low-compute regimes.

papers.title: Which Text Matters: Handling Model Uncertainty in Text-as-Data Regressions, with an Application to Central Bank Communication
papers.summary: Social scientists routinely convert text into covariates like topic shares, ideal points or sentiment scores, and insert them into statistical models of interest. This two-step design is convenient, but it is rarely guided by theory: little tells the analyst which text-based covariates to construct or include. Each approach embodies contestable measurement choices, and competing operationalizations of the same construct can support different conclusions, so a single research question gives rise to a menu of competing regression models. Which text constructed covariates belong in a model, and in what functional form, is thus a problem of model uncertainty. We propose spike-and-slab generalized additive models (SSGAMs), which jointly select covariates and determine whether their effects are linear or nonlinear. We illustrate the approach with the communication of a powerful unelected institution, asking which of 45 competing text indicators from 224 monthly European Central Bank press conferences, spanning late 2002 to mid-2025, track professional inflation expectations. A sparse set is selected; widely used alternatives, and every tested nonlinear effect, carry no incremental information.

papers.title: No Way To Steal My Face: Proactive Defense Against Identity-Preserving Personalized Generation
papers.summary: Recent advances in diffusion models have enabled high-fidelity, identity-preserving image generation for personalized applications such as digital avatars and virtual try-on systems. However, their reliance on sensitive facial reference images raises growing privacy concerns. Existing defense mechanisms are primarily designed for training-based personalization and struggle to generalize to emerging training-free approaches, due to fundamental differences in their identity integration paradigms. To bridge this gap, we propose IDGuardian-the first generalizable and model-agnostic identity protection framework capable of defending against both training-based and training-free personalization methods. IDGuardian abstracts the personalization process into two critical stages: identity extraction and identity injection. It then introduces crafted adversarial perturbations to simultaneously disrupt both stages. Specifically, it degrades the identity features extracted by external encoders and establishes an adversarial conceptual bridge that misdirects the generative trajectory away from the target identity. Extensive experiments show that IDGuardian effectively protects identity across various personalization pipelines and model architectures, while remaining robust to post-processing, adaptive attacks, and cross-dataset generalization. Our code is available at https://github.com/OpenAscent-L/IDGuardian.git.

papers.title: A catalog of long, eccentric and precessing binary black hole simulations from ICTS-TIFR
papers.summary: We present a catalogue of 31 binary black hole simulations performed with the Spectral Einstein Code (SpEC) on the Sonic cluster at ICTS-TIFR, Bengaluru between August 2023 and December 2024, targeting the sparsely covered corner of parameter space in which orbital eccentricity and spin-orbit precession are present simultaneously: 17 configurations are both eccentric and precessing, spanning mass ratios $1 \le q \le 11$ and initial eccentricities up to $\hat{e}_0 = 0.40$. The longest, EccPrecDiff002, inspirals for 80 orbits (159 gravitational-wave cycles), to our knowledge the longest simultaneously eccentric and precessing binary black hole evolution to date. Compile-time optimisation of SpEC and its third-party library stack for the AMD Zen-2 architecture delivered a 90% speedup of the initial-data solver and a 40% speedup of the evolution, roughly half of the latter traceable to a single defect in how pre-2.34 glibc reported cache topology on AMD processors. The campaign consumed $1.18 \times 10^{6}$ CPU-hours. We document the post-processing pipeline and validate the frame transformation and waveforms. Eccentricity is measured from the waveforms and compared against the initial data. The first law of binary black hole mechanics, a test of approximate helical symmetry, is satisfied to better than 0.54% for every configuration with $e_ω < 0.2$, and we show that even precessing systems can be regarded as possessing approximate helical symmetry in the co-precessing frame. Using the aligned-spin simulations to calibrate the numerical floor, the co-precessing approximation's mirror-symmetry violation lies three to four ordersof magnitude above it, growing from 0.7% to 5.3%with opening angle. EccPrecDiff002 spans the band above 5 Hz without hybridisationfor $M \le 62\,M_\odot$, giving a single-interferometer signal-to-noise ratio of 961 in Cosmic Explorer at 1 Gpc.

papers.title: Hierarchical Parameter Estimation for Intrinsic Parameters of Extreme-mass-ratio Inspirals Using Deep Learning
papers.summary: Extreme-mass-ratio inspirals (EMRIs) stand as prime targets for future space-borne gravitational wave (GW) detectors, yet their precise parameter estimation is severely hindered by waveform complexity and high-dimensional parameter spaces. In this work, we propose a deep learning framework capable of recovering the seven intrinsic EMRI parameters without relying on detailed priors for extrinsic parameters. Our approach first employs a U-Net to extract robust signal features from noisy time-frequency data. These features are then fed into a multi-channel convolutional neural network (CNN) equipped with a dual attention mechanism, which decouples the time and frequency dimensions to jointly model long-range temporal evolution and persistent spectral structures, thereby enhancing sensitivity to EMRI time-frequency ridges in noisy data. Remarkably, this method reduces the search ranges for the parameters $\{\log M, a, μ, e_0, p_0 \}$ and $\{t_p, {x_I}_0 \}$ by factors of $\sim 10^{2}$ and $\sim 10^{1}$, respectively, effectively shrinking the total volume of the seven-dimensional parameter space by $\sim 10^{8}$. Such a dramatic reduction enables a rapid pre-screening of the intrinsic parameter space, substantially saving computational cost for subsequent full parameter estimation. Although our framework is developed with Taiji mission specifications in mind, the methodology is applicable to data from other space-borne GW detectors.

papers.title: Probing the production mechanisms of virtual photons at RHIC
papers.summary: We report the measurement of direct virtual photon ($γ^*_\text{dir} \rightarrow e^+e^-$) in four Au+Au collision energies at $\sqrt{s_\text{NN}}$ = 14.6--54.4 GeV. The $γ^*_\text{dir}$ yields scale with charged-particle multiplicity ($(dN_{\mathrm{ch}}/dη)^α$) as $α=1.43 \pm 0.04 \text{(stat.)} \pm 0.03\text{(sys.)}$, independent of collision energies and centralities, exceeding hadronic expectations and indicating notable contribution from QGP phase. At $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=$ 54.4 GeV, the direct virtual photon mass distributions are further studied over $0.1 < M_{ee} < 1.1$ GeV/$c^2$, and are found to evolve from exponential to power-law form with increasing $p_\text{T}$, signaling a shift from "blackbody" radiation to emission governed by Kroll-Wada formalism.

papers.title: SULA: Robust Langevin Sampling via Drift-Diffusion Saturation
papers.summary: The unadjusted Langevin algorithm (ULA) and its stochastic-gradient variant, SGLD, are workhorses of modern Bayesian machine learning, but can be fragile when faced with a target distribution possessing a non-Lipschitz drift. In such settings, the expected squared jump distance can grow rapidly, leading to numerical instability or the need for prohibitively small step-sizes. We propose the saturated unadjusted Langevin algorithm (SULA) that pairs a saturated gradient drift with a gradient-informed state-dependent diffusion, while preserving first-order consistency with the Langevin diffusion. The drift and diffusion terms are chosen to guarantee that the one-step squared update is independent of the gradient. Consequently, SULA is robust to the choice of step-size and preserves estimation and prediction quality. We provide sufficient conditions under which SULA with a step-size $h$ converges weakly to the Langevin diffusion at the standard $O(h)$ rate, the SULA chain is geometrically ergodic, and that the bias of its invariant measure relative to the target is $O(h)$. Further, we develop SG-SULA, a stochastic-gradient version of SULA that rescales the stochastic gradient using a Gaussian CDF correction under Gaussianity of the gradient noise. Numerical experiments on various examples demonstrate SULA's robustness to tuning and SG-SULA's improved predictive performance.

papers.title: Measuring and Reducing Unusable Replies of LLM Agents
papers.summary: People delegate multi-step work to LLM agents and read only the reply that the agent hands back. Current evaluation scores task completion and the faithfulness of reports, and it leaves open whether the requester can understand and use the reply. We call this property reply usability and measure it with a reader model that takes the requester's position and tests whether the reply can be interpreted from what the requester has seen, is in the requester's language and answers the request. Its agreement with the majority of five annotators lies within the range of the individual annotators. Across eight models from seven families, 54% of 480 replies fail, and the best model still fails on 30%. Failed replies mostly point to material the requester has not seen or use labels that the agent coined during its work. Stating explicit requirements for the reply reduces the failure rate from 0.52 to 0.43 together with errors and omissions, and a secondary model that rewrites the reply reduces it to 0.36, which human annotators confirm in a blind comparison. Reply usability can thus be scored alongside task success and improved with one appended message or one call to a secondary model.

papers.title: AWARE-RG: Abstraction Aware Explanation of Resiliency Graphs for Cyber Physical Systems
papers.summary: Understanding the security posture of cyber physical systems (CPS) requires reasoning across both information technology (IT) and operational technology (OT). However, a security analyst often holds an incomplete, role-specific view of the underlying system which has most likely resulted from their knowledge limited by a need-to-know framework. Such an incomplete view can potentially lead them to incorrectly assess if a cyber attack produces an untoward physical consequence resulting in making uninformed decisions about system resilience. In this work, we present AWARE-RG (Abstraction Aware Explanation of Resiliency Graphs), a semi-automated, human-in-the-loop framework that provides an analyst with a role-bounded, need-to-know explanations of resiliency paths in a CPS. The AWARE-RG abstraction structure is derived using Formal Concept Analysis over MITRE ATT&CK for ICS tactics, ordered by the ICS Cyber Kill Chain. For valid attack-fault queries, plan repair and backward means-end analysis identify the missing dependencies, explain why the physical hazard is reachable, and suggest defensive strategies. For invalid attack-fault queries, AWARE-RG localizes the first abstraction level at which the path fails, and reports confirmed blocking conditions as hardening pointers.

papers.title: Model-Induced Hazard Geometry and Functional Representations in Survival Analysis
papers.summary: Individualized survival predictions are often summarized by scalar risk scores or event probabilities at selected time horizons, although clinically relevant risk may also differ in its temporal organization. We consider finite-dimensional representations of individual hazard trajectories through interpretable hazard functionals, such as peak timing, cumulative hazard over prespecified intervals, and persistence of elevated risk. A central issue is that the richness of such representations is constrained by the hazard geometry supported by the underlying survival model. We formalize this through model-induced tangent spaces and functional ranks, derive an exact decomposition of model-supported variation into directions retained and lost by a chosen representation, and introduce a model-relative notion of local completeness. We further distinguish intrinsic model capacity from the variation actually activated by covariates. These results motivate a structured extension of AFT time scaling through a positive-affine deformation on the log-time scale, yielding a power-warp mechanism with an additional temporal deformation direction. Combined with a log-logistic reference hazard, this gives a parsimonious likelihood-based working specification for which peak timing and peak height provide complete coordinates over the unimodal regime. We also establish plug-in recovery and asymptotic inference for hazard functionals. Simulations and a lung-cancer application illustrate how model-induced restrictions propagate to hazard-functional representations.

papers.title: "The Rose Garden Is a Cemetery": Spatial Dissonance and Divergent Public Experiences of an Indigenous Augmented Reality Tour
papers.summary: Community-authored augmented reality (AR) can contest dominant heritage narratives by juxtaposing stories with physical surroundings. We examine the Thámien Ohlone AR Tour, developed with members of the Ohlone Native American community at Mission Santa Clara and Santa Clara University. Combining paired pre/post surveys from 57 participants with collaborative thematic analysis, we compare reception among Ohlone community members, university affiliates, and Mission visitors. Spatial dissonance captures felt tensions when AR challenged familiar campus readings or when surroundings conflicted with Ohlone histories the AR affirmed, such as a garden's significance as a burial ground. Cultural frames shaped interpretation; contemporary people and relationships made Ohlone continuance tangible. Participants appreciated the tour and called for permanent physical acknowledgment. We propose staging reflective encounters, clarifying community-authored meanings, and using AR to prototype public acknowledgment and support community-directed advocacy. These findings foreground relationships to land and place, informed by Indigenous scholarship, in designing and evaluating AR.
papers.comment: 26 pages. Preprint. Submitted to CHI 2027. Survey instrument and fieldwork protocol included as ancillary files

papers.title: Collective-flow signatures of bubble nuclei in intermediate-energy projectile fragmentation reactions
papers.summary: Characterized by central density depletion, bubble nuclei represent an important class of exotic nuclear structures. Collective flow in the $^{40}$Ca+$^{9}$Be projectile fragmentation reaction at 140 MeV/u is investigated using the extended quantum molecular dynamics (EQMD) model with a parameter on of the isoscalar monopole excitation strength $\varepsilon$. The projectile $^{40}Ca$ is initialized as a relaxed ten-$α$ cluster configuration exhibiting a bubble-like density distribution. The results reveal that increasing $\varepsilon$ modifies the density distribution and the size of the depleted central region of bubble, producing pronounced changes in fragment yields and collective flow around $\varepsilon\approx0.5$. Below this value, heavy-fragment production plays a significant role, while the directed flow $v_1$ of protons and neutrons remains predominantly negative, indicating preferential emission toward the target side. Above $\varepsilon\approx0.5$, enhanced expansion of the central low-density region suppresses heavy residues and drives $v_1$ toward positive values. In contrast, preformed $α$ clusters show different responses, reflecting their origin in the initial cluster configuration rather than solely in secondary decay. At low excitation, the cluster flow exhibits a pronounced impact-parameter dependence, whereas stronger excitation weakens cluster binding and suppresses directional anisotropy, driving the flow close to zero. The rapidity slopes of the flow coefficients also vary systematically with $\varepsilon$, tracing changes in emission anisotropy during expansion. These findings extend traditional static descriptions by probing the dynamical evolution of exotic structures in heavy-ion reactions and the contrasting collective-flow behavior of preformed clusters and single nucleons constitutes a sensitive dynamical probe of bubble-like structures.

papers.title: Tidal deformability of white dwarfs in Eddington-inspired Born-Infeld gravity
papers.summary: We compute the static quadrupole Love number $k_2$ and the dimensionless tidal deformability $Λ$ of cold white dwarfs in Eddington-inspired Born-Infeld (EiBI) gravity. Matter couples to the physical metric while perturbation equations are solved in an auxiliary metric, so the physical tidal field near the surface depends on derivatives of the equation of state. This dependence is regular for a surface polytropic index $1<Γ_{\rm env}<3/2$, but not for the $Γ= 5/3$ Chandrasekhar equation of state. The mechanism, an algebraic map between the metric that carries perturbations and the metric that matter feels, is common to Palatini-type theories, so the same type of surface condition should apply to tidal calculations in this wider class. We use thermodynamically consistent envelopes that exactly reach zero enthalpy. At five masses from \(0.6\) to \(1.3\,\Msun\) and five sampled Born-Infeld couplings \(κ\), with $|κ|\le5\times10^6\,\mathrm{m^2}$, the EiBI-GR differences are approximately linear in $κ$. The largest absolute fractional shifts are \(3.89\times 10^{-5}\) in the stellar radius $R$, \(4.09\times 10^{-5}\) in $k_2$, and \(2.36\times 10^{-4}\) in $Λ$. Across nine envelope models, half the spread of each quantity relative to the baseline envelope is at most \(0.0186\) in $R$ and \(0.0857\) in \(k_2\), but only \(3.02\times 10^{-5}\) in \(Λ\) as the changes in \(k_2\) and \(R^5\) largely cancel. A high-precision calculation shows that the envelope dependence of the EiBI-GR difference in \(Λ\) is small. Half the spread of this difference ranges from \(1.067\times 10^{-12}\) to \(6.208\times 10^{-11}\) over the 20 nonzero mass-coupling points.

papers.title: A quantum probabilistic approach to the emergence of an inflationary Starobinsky Universe
papers.summary: We propose that the necessary conditions for the existence of inflation could be explained by a quantum probabilistic approach. We interpret physical states $ψ$ obtained via the path integral formulation as probability density amplitudes for the Universe to be measured at a particular geometric configuration. First, we examine the problem of ordering ambiguities in the Wheeler-DeWitt (WDW) equation. We develop a formalism to handle ambiguities in the canonical quantization of a $1d$ minisuperspace by defining ambiguity functions within the WDW equation. We define a Hilbert space inner product for calculating physical observables, and using an argument from the hermiticity of the Hamiltonian, we obtain an expression for its measure $μ$ in addition to constraints on the ambiguity functions. By defining a new quantum state $Ψ=\sqrtμ ψ$ and using the path integral formalism, we are able to resolve ambiguities and prove the theory is universal. We then generalize for any $M$-dimensional minisuperspace system, for which we can prove universality in the semi-classical approximation for a large class of models. We also show that this universality extends to all orders of quantum theory if the target space manifold of the theory is flat. We calculate probability amplitudes for various cosmological scenarios involving Starobinsky inflation. We summarize the Hartle-Hawking no-boundary proposal for GR and we comment on the distinct possibilities of defining a contour of integration: the sign choice of Hartle-Hawking vs that of Linde-Vilenkin. We make an analogous calculation for $R^{2}$ gravity and find that for the Linde- Vilenkin choice it is statistically more likely for the Universe to emerge in its inflationary stage. Finally, we calculate transition amplitudes when the kinetic energy of the inflaton field $φ$ takes non-zero values.
papers.comment: PhD thesis defended on 20 January 2026; 4+166 pages

papers.title: A Graph-Based Analysis of Comparability, Scale, and Attribution in Private Transformer Inference
papers.summary: Rising privacy concerns around large language models have accelerated research in private Transformer inference (PTI). Synthesizing the empirical claims in this line of research, however, is hindered by multi-dimensional cryptographic progress and inconsistent evaluation contracts. In this work, we systematize the field by constructing an empirical graph of 62 PTI systems, mapping system attributes to node features and evaluation compatibility to edges. A three-tiered analysis of this graph illuminates the state of private inference. Node-level attribution shows that cryptographic progress drives performance gains across most systems, yet always co-occurs with other factors (model fidelity, hardware, cost accounting). Edge-level auditing shows that only 1 of 1891 candidate system pairs is directly comparable under shared assumptions. Finally, graph-level analysis shows that the scaling frontier of private inference has plateaued at 13B parameters and projects the cost of deploying current PTI techniques on production-scale Transformers. Overall, this graph-based framework equips the community to evaluate PTI claims transparently and channel technical speedups into deployment-scale private inference.

papers.title: Mission (Im)Possible: Towards Autonomous Discovery of Autopilot Logic Flaws in Open-Source Drone Frameworks
papers.summary: Autonomous drones are increasingly deployed in safety-critical tasks, yet their autopilot software can still contain subtle logic flaws that lead to unsafe behaviors. These flaws are difficult to discover with existing techniques because they often depend on semantic relationships across modules, commands, and runtime state, and rarely manifest as crashes or detectable failures. With recent advances in LLMs, we observe that, when equipped with essential domain knowledge and carefully crafted context, LLMs demonstrate strong capabilities in understanding the high-level semantics of autopilot systems, making them suitable for logic flaw discovery. However, LLMs are limited by their context and can be biased to the vulnerabilities frequently occurs in training dataset, while logic flaws often require higher-level semantic bug oracles to identify their existence. To bridge the gap, we present Impossible Mission Finder (IMF), a multi-agent system combining static analysis, dynamic execution and log analysis, that supports fully automated identify, test, and validate logic flaws in autonomous vehicles. IMF primarily contains three LLM agents, it first uses the auditor agent to propose logic flaw hypothesis based on carefully-crafted program slicing, then it launches tester agents to write and execute test cases for each candidate, and finally it spawns the log analyzer agent to validate the execution log against the flaw hypothesis. This enables IMF dynamically validate bug oracles in a case-by-case manner, making it suitable for discovering logic flaws that do not have a unified pattern. We evaluated IMF on two widely used open-source autopilot systems, PX4 and Ardupilot, leading to 105 previously unknown logic flaws, that can cause unsafe behaviors including mission interruption failures, invalid actions, entering into restricted fly zones etc.

papers.title: R-process nuclei in the rare-earth region above N=126 in Relativistic Hartree-Bogoliubov theory: A preponderance of shape-coexistence in nuclei
papers.summary: The shell structure of nuclei beyond N=126 relevant to the third peak at A ~ 195 in r-process nuclear abundances in investigated. Within the framework of the relativistic Hartree-Bogoliubov theory in deformed space, a comparative study of the response of nuclei with three different model Lagrangians NL-SV1, SVI-2 and NL3 is made. Ground-state properties of even-even nuclei in the isotopic chains of Z=58-72$= in the highly neutron-rich region are investigated. A comparison of binding energies with mass formulas shows that in the extreme region of the r-process path, the RMF model SVI-2 without nonlinearities of sigma and omega mesons shows an excellent agreement with the mass formula HFB-24. It is shown that in all the above Lagrangian models, in the neutron rich region between the shell closures N=126 and N=184, there is a preponderance of nuclides exhibiting coexistence of well-deformed prolate and oblate shapes in the ground state. A prolate ground state is shown to evolve smoothly to a coexisting oblate ground state via a near degeneracy with successive addition of neutrons. Induced by an onset of deformation for $N \ge 130$, nuclei approaching the r-process path are shown to exhibit enhanced stability in many isotopic chains (Z > 60). This has the effect of shifting the expected neutron drip line significantly farther into the neutron-rich region especially for the higher Z chains. Consequences of the enhanced stability, the shape co-existence and degeneracy of shapes in nuclei on the r-process nucleosynthesis are discussed.

papers.title: Nambu's Dynamics, Strings and Gravitized Quantum Theory
papers.summary: In this article we present a new view on string theory that is rooted in quantum foundations extended to the domain of quantum gravity in the form of gravitized quantum theory, in which the canonical probability measure captured by the Born rule of quantum theory, turns out to be dynamical and contextual. We claim that this gravitization of quantum theory is the essence of string theory. String theory, according to this view, originates in foundations of quantum theory and Nambu's dynamics, which features in the non-perturbative definition of string theory in terms of a T-duality covariant and non-commutative formulation, called the metastring. Nambu's dynamics and the associated cubic and hypercubic objects also appear as the natural language for exploring the new observables and phenomena implied by a dynamical Born rule, including triple and higher order quantum interference, that can be investigated in experiments involving massive quantum probes, and that are also needed for direct empirical tests of the Born rule, a cornerstone of quantum theory.

papers.title: Detectability of Gravitational Waves from Extreme-Mass-Ratio Inspirals on Periodic Orbits around Bardeen Black Holes
papers.summary: We investigate gravitational wave (GW) signatures from extreme-mass-ratio inspirals (EMRIs) around a Bardeen black hole, modeling the small object as a test particle, and provide a framework for probing strong-field spacetime geometry. We first present the equations of motion for test particles around a Bardeen black hole and characterize circular orbits in the parameter space of energy and angular momentum. Using Levin's classification, we adopt the extended classification scheme to classify periodic orbits around a Bardeen black hole. We then compute GW waveforms in both the time and frequency domains, as well as the corresponding characteristic strains, for these periodic orbits and compare them with the sensitivity curves of the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA), the evolved Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (eLISA), the TianQin mission, the Big Bang Observer (BBO), and the Decihertz Interferometer Gravitational wave Observatory (DECIGO). We find that detectability is controlled primarily by the luminosity distance. At a luminosity distance of 200 Mpc, the signals can exceed the sensitivity curves of BBO and DECIGO and are comparable to the LISA sensitivity curve, whereas at 2 Gpc, they remain below the sensitivity curves of all detectors considered. These results suggest that EMRIs on periodic orbits around Bardeen black holes offer a promising avenue to probe strong-field gravity and the properties of Bardeen black holes.

papers.title: Building a Sovereign Benchmark The Limits of Private Coordination
papers.summary: Public debt supplies liquidity and collateral services only if institutions coordinate on using the same claim. We study this coordination when use carries a recurring cost and a benefit that rises with other users. Above a quality threshold, two positive-adoption equilibria exist, and under best responses the initial user base decides between collapse and high adoption. Under logit choice, as the population grows and noise vanishes, the long-run distribution selects high adoption only above a strictly higher threshold. Debt issuance improves market depth but eventually dilutes backing per claim. This trade-off creates a range of debt levels supporting the liquidity premium of public debt in macroeconomic models and a narrower range supporting its long-run selection. At the boundary of the wider range, the premium is discontinuous. A matching transfer that corrects the adoption externality makes stationary selection maximize network surplus. Transfers can also help launch a network without permanent support.

papers.title: Rewarding Noise: Incentives in Decentralized A/B Testing
papers.summary: Many firms that run A/B tests struggle with low statistical power, increasing the risk that launch decisions are driven by noise rather than true impact. We argue that in decentralized organizations, low power can reflect misaligned incentives: product teams choose what and how to test on a customer-facing experience to maximize their private reward, while the experience owner sets evaluation rules and launch criteria to optimize the experience. We formalize this interaction via a principal-agent model and show that evaluating tests using raw impact estimates creates a reward to sampling noise. Correctly calibrated posterior-mean evaluation removes this reward and creates a local incentive to reallocate toward fewer, more precise tests of more ambitious ideas. Using data on A/B tests run at Amazon, we document patterns consistent with these model predictions. After an Amazon experience shifted to posterior-mean-based evaluation in 2024, test volume declined while both precision and the dispersion of true impacts increased, more than doubling signal-to-noise ratios. Our results highlight that A/B testing methodologies can shape not only measurement and launch decisions, but which tests are pursued in the first place.

papers.title: Structure Before Intelligence: Gating What Agentic Scientific Workflows Release
papers.summary: An agentic scientific workflow can run to completion and still release wrong results: a silent numerical error, a stale input, or a defect in a shared upstream step can contaminate several outputs while a sibling branch stays correct. We treat trust in such results as a release decision. A harness around the workflow's directed acyclic graph (DAG) decides which outputs may be used: it enforces mandatory checks, contains failures to the affected branch, recomputes from tracked versions, adds validators, and releases a result only if a risk model estimates its probability of being invalid as low. Language-model agents work inside the harness, choosing corrective actions and reviewing releases, but cannot override it. On 60 held-out paired instances of two workflows with injected faults, we switched components on and off. Each supplied a different property. Containment and recovery raised the number of correct results. Validation supplied safety: fixed rules without validation released 37 invalid results, while validating every candidate released none. Risk estimation supplied efficiency, matching that safety with 31% fewer validators at somewhat lower yield, although better targeting than random validation was not shown. Lineage evidence helped on one workflow. The language model added no measurable benefit: whether invalid results escaped depended on the harness, not the model. This proof of concept points to a practical path: placing agents inside explicit release-control structure can keep released scientific results trustworthy, and it gives more capable agents a measurable baseline to improve on.
papers.comment: 21 pages: 10-page main paper and 11-page supplement; 2 figures

papers.title: Superhorizon enhancement of the hydrodynamic GW tail in Standard Model embedded warm inflation
papers.summary: Hydrodynamic fluctuations in the primordial plasma generate a gravitational-wave (GW) background that grows like $f^3_\mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle 0}$ in terms of the current frequency. However, within the ($10^{-4}_{ } ... 10^4_{ })\,$Hz band of upcoming interferometers, the modes likely re-entered the Hubble horizon when the hydrodynamic noise was no longer at its maximal value. To address this situation, we define a model-independent transfer function for GWs generated by hydrodynamic (or other white-noise) fluctuations at any time. Employing appropriate variables, we show how this transfer function, together with the simpler vacuum one, can be determined numerically for a general expansion history. The results are illustrated for Standard Model embedded warm inflation scenarios, including both the vacuum and hydrodynamic parts. Following previous estimates, we find that a pre-exit-generated hydrodynamic tail becomes almost flat below $(10^5_{ } ... 10^7_{ })\;$Hz. Its small-$f^{ }_\mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle 0}$ intercept remains finite, and can then moderately influence observational constraints through the tensor-to-scalar ratio ($r$).

papers.title: What You Sign Is Not What You Run: The Verifiability Gap in Quantized LLM Supply Chains
papers.summary: Model signing authenticates the full-precision weights W an LLM is released with, yet users run a quantized artifact Q whose producing transformation is not uniquely determined under current disclosure. We separate the non-environment inputs from the execution environment E and measure a quantity that, to our knowledge, has not been measured before: the Independent Verifiability Rate (IVR), the fraction of a popularity-sampled GGUF ecosystem that a third party can re-derive bit-for-bit. Across the 200 most-downloaded Hugging Face GGUF repositories (198 in scope), no artifact or model card records the build environment, so under a recorded-inputs protocol the IVR is 0/198. Yet the artifacts are not irreproducible. On four in-sample repositories that disclose their inputs, the card's information alone reproduces no Q4_K_M file, but two coordinates the card omits - the build's floating-point-contraction setting and, for hybrid models, the per-tensor quantization recipe - re-derive 7/8 target-quant files bit-for-bit on x86 (5/8 on arm64); the fp16 re-derives from the provider's checkpoint, but the calibration imatrix must be shipped and hash-bound, since recomputing it did not match. An older release additionally pins the instruction set and did not re-derive. Reproducing the divergence reported with llama.cpp PR #25353, we show that E is a necessary coordinate and that one compiler setting yields a unique output across the tested platforms at negligible quality cost (+0.06% perplexity). As a security characterization, benign floating-point non-determinism separates from uniformly placed nibble-flip tampering above a detection floor that grows with the environments a verifier must allow, but a targeted embedding edit evades the statistic, so the proposed protocol rests on exact re-derivation; adversarial-fp16 attacks lie outside it. We release the audit data and a re-runnable harness.

papers.title: Who Keeps a Bubble Alive? Skin in the Game and the Survival of Rational Bubbles
papers.summary: We study how retained ownership supports the value of an asset that pays no dividends and is held only for resale. A sponsor chooses hidden maintenance that determines market survival, bears its full cost, and captures only the benefit accruing to its retained tokens. A positive stationary equilibrium exists if and only if retention meets an endogenous minimum. Under additional curvature restrictions, retention above this threshold supports two positive stationary equilibria. Conditional on survival, prices below the upper equilibrium converge to the lower one while the upper price is the largest feasible initial valuation. Greater retention expands the feasible price interval. Credible news that future retention will be below the minimum causes an immediate collapse through backward unraveling. The model identifies a governance channel through which insider unlocks can affect valuation without changing total token supply or fundamental cash flows.

papers.title: Quantum-Resilient Secure Protocol for Decentralized Edge-IoT Peer-to-Peer Energy Trading Systems
papers.summary: The rise of quantum computing presents substantial challenges to the security of Peer-to-Peer (P2P) energy trading systems. This paper introduces an innovative mutual authenticated session key agreement protocol aimed at protecting edge-IoT P2P energy trading communications in the quantum era. Each peer is an IoT-enabled smart metering device that is registered by an edge registration authority and acts as both producer and consumer. The proposed protocol incorporates CRYSTALS-Kyber's quantum-resistant cryptographic suite to guarantee the authenticity and confidentiality of negotiated session keys in the presence of quantum threats. Furthermore, it leverages the Hedera Hashgraph public blockchain, which is recognized for its quantum-resilient design, to ensure transparency and support efficient revocation mechanisms. Extensive comparative analyses have been conducted to demonstrate the protocol's superiority over existing alternatives, including both traditional schemes based on classical cryptography and emerging early-stage post-quantum approaches, in terms of performance and security features. By combining robust security and high efficiency, the proposed protocol fosters the development of resilient decentralized energy markets, paving the way for secure and sustainable energy distribution in the future.

papers.title: How Long Is the Coast of a Neuron? Resolution-Dependent Interaction Order and Computational Capacity
papers.summary: Mandlebrot's coastline paradox reframes measurement as a joint property of an object and its ruler. Here we ask how observational resolution shapes the apparent structure of neural computation. We introduce a scale-indexed decomposition that separates the predictive information captured by direct dependencies from the residual outside that model family. Exact constructions show that projection can convert higher-order dependence into pairwise structure. Projection can increase the direct fraction of surviving information even as total predictive information decreases. A schematic branch-to-soma cascade grounds these effects in local coincidence detection, saturating integration and somatic mixing. Resolving organized nonlinear subunits improves approximation and raises effective representational rank. In a nested hierarchy, these gains occur without increasing information about the target. This distinction separates information availability from access by a restricted readout. A point-neuron or direct population model therefore establishes an effective description at a specified scale. It does not uniquely identify the finer computation that generated the observed relation. Which resolution is adequate depends on the observable and perturbation of interest.

papers.title: Binding energies in the $0^{-+}$ and $1^{--}$ fermion--antifermion channels from the ladder Bethe-Salpeter and Schrödinger equations
